  The same analyses with pedigree BLUP (A^-1), GBLUP (G^-1) or single-step

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

[中文版](relationship-matrices-zh.html)

Every function of mintyrasr takes the inverse relationship matrix in the
argument `ginv` and puts it into `vm(id, ginv)`. Which information the model
uses is decided only by the matrix you pass:

| method | matrix | built from | individuals with a prediction |
|---|---|---|---|
| pedigree BLUP (ABLUP) | A^-1 | pedigree | everyone in the pedigree |
| GBLUP | G^-1 | genotypes | genotyped individuals |
| single-step GBLUP (ssGBLUP) | H^-1 | pedigree + genotypes | everyone in the pedigree |

Nothing else changes: scenarios, models, outputs and tests are the same.

## Building the matrices

```{r}
library(asreml)
library(ASRgenomics)

# A^-1 from the pedigree (id, sire, dam; parents before offspring, 0 / NA = unknown)
ainv <- ainverse(ped)            # sparse, carries rowNames, INVERSE and inbreeding

# G^-1 from a marker matrix (individuals x SNPs, coded 0/1/2)
G    <- G.matrix(M = M, method = "VanRaden")$G
ginv <- G.inverse(G = G, sparseform = TRUE)$Ginv.sparse

# H^-1: G must be aligned to the pedigree relationships of the genotyped
# animals (A22) first, and the genotyped animals must be in the pedigree.
# See ?G.tuneup, ?match.G2A and ?H.inverse in your ASRgenomics version for the
# exact arguments; the result must carry INVERSE = TRUE and rowNames.
hinv <- H.inverse(A = A, Ginv = Ginv_aligned, lambda = 1, sparseform = TRUE)
```

All three must carry `attr(, "INVERSE") = TRUE`; mintyrasr warns otherwise,
because `vm()` would then use the matrix as the relationship matrix itself.

## What mintyrasr sets for you

- **`dense = "auto"`**: the relationship term goes into `dense` for a (nearly)
  full inverse such as G^-1 or H^-1, and not for a sparse A^-1, where it would
  cost a lot of memory. The choice is shown in the first progress line.
- **Inbreeding for the reliability** `1 - PEV / ((1 + F) Va)`: with `ainverse()`
  F is taken from its `inbreeding` attribute when `inbreeding = NULL`. For G
  use `diag(G) - 1`; for H the pedigree F of `ainverse()` is the usual choice.
- The output file names carry the name of the matrix object
  (`st_sp_ainv.xlsx`, `st_sp_ginv.xlsx`, ...), or the method name in
  `asr_compare()`.

## One method

```{r}
library(mintyr)
library(mintyrasr)

sc <- cv_scenarios(pheno, cols = c("adg", "bf"), id = "id", group = "test_herd",
                   v = 5, repeats = 5, seed = 2026, out_type = "df")

res_a <- asr_scenarios(sc, ainv, fixed = ~ hhys)                       # ABLUP, F from ainverse()
res_g <- asr_scenarios(sc, ginv, fixed = ~ hhys, inbreeding = F_genomic) # GBLUP
```

## Comparing the methods

`asr_compare()` runs the same scenarios with each matrix and stacks the
results with a `method` column. All methods use the same folds, so the
comparison is paired:

```{r}
cmp <- asr_compare(sc, list(ABLUP = ainv, GBLUP = ginv, ssGBLUP = hinv),
                   scenarios = c("st_sp", "st_mp"), fixed = ~ hhys, dir = "compare",
                   inbreeding = list(GBLUP = F_genomic))
cmp$param                       # h2 (+ SE) per method and scenario
cmp$summary[type == "pa"]       # predictive ability per method
# compare/compare.xlsx and one workbook per scenario and method
```

A compact table of PA by method:

```{r}
library(data.table)
dcast(cmp$summary[type == "pa"], scenario + name + test_herd ~ method, value.var = "mean")
```

## Points to watch

- **Which animals are in the data.** GBLUP can only use genotyped animals.
  For a fair comparison, validate all methods on the same (genotyped)
  individuals; ABLUP and ssGBLUP can additionally use non-genotyped animals
  with records in the training sets.
- **IDs must match** between the phenotypes, the pedigree and the genotypes;
  mintyrasr warns about phenotyped individuals that are not in the matrix.
- **ssGBLUP needs a compatible G**: align G to A22 (scale and level) before
  building H, otherwise the genomic and pedigree parts do not fit together and
  predictions are biased - visible as a slope far from 1.
